title: All Departments Including Those with No Employees
description:
Use a RIGHT JOIN so that **every department appears** in the result, even if it has no employees yet.

**Table: employees** — `id`, `name`, `department_id`
**Table: departments** — `id`, `name`

Return the department `name` aliased as `department` and the `employee_count` (0 for departments with no staff). Order by `department`.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE departments (id INT, name VARCHAR); CREATE TABLE employees (id INT, name VARCHAR, department_id INT); INSERT INTO departments VALUES (1,'Engineering'),(2,'Sales'),(3,'HR'),(4,'Marketing'),(5,'Finance'); INSERT INTO employees VALUES (1,'Alice',1),(2,'Bob',1),(3,'Carol',2),(4,'Dave',3),(5,'Eve',1);
solution_sql: SELECT d.name AS department, COUNT(e.id) AS employee_count FROM employees e RIGHT JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.id GROUP BY d.id, d.name ORDER BY d.name

test_cases.description: All 5 departments returned; Marketing and Finance have employee_count = 0

hints: RIGHT JOIN keeps all rows from the right table (departments) even when there is no matching employee.
Use COUNT(e.id) not COUNT(*) — counting a column skips NULLs, giving 0 for empty departments.
explanation: A RIGHT JOIN ensures every department row appears. Departments 4 (Marketing) and 5 (Finance) have no employees, so e.id is NULL for those rows. COUNT(e.id) skips NULLs and returns 0 for those departments, while COUNT(*) would incorrectly return 1.
